clue.text: Probably not one of Roger Fry's Transformations

definitions.text: Probably not one of Roger Fry's Transformations

parts.words: Probably not one of Roger Fry's Transformations
parts.note: Roger Fry's essay collection Transformations is about art; the answer is a transformation of quite another kind, the chemical change inside living bodies

explanation.surface: A remark on the contents of the art critic Roger Fry's book Transformations.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Fry, the Bloomsbury art critic, published Transformations (1926), essays on art. The answer is a bodily transformation, so it would hardly be one of his.
explanation.definitionFit: The body's chemistry continually converts food into energy and tissue, a biological transformation rather than an aesthetic one.

clue.text: "Another man … carries her — , in which is her little lap-dog" (Fanny Burney, Diary)

definitions.text: "Another man … carries her — , in which is her little lap-dog" (Fanny Burney, Diary)

parts.words: "Another man … carries her — , in which is her little lap-dog" (Fanny Burney, Diary)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the fur hand-warmer a lady of Burney's day carried, big enough to hold a small dog

explanation.surface: A line from Fanny Burney's diary with one word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney's diary describes a servant carrying a lady's fur hand-warmer with her lap-dog inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank needs a tubular fur warmer for the hands, the kind of fashionable accessory in which a lap-dog could ride.

clue.text: Melody, a French one after tea, we are told

indicators.note: after places the French word behind the letter from tea
what we are told is heard spoken, so the drink is taken as the sound of a letter name

parts.note: the drink tea sounds like the letter T
une is French for a or one (feminine)

explanation.surface: A tune sung in French after afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we are told' turns the drink tea into the letter T, which sounds the same; 'after' puts UNE behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune is a sequence of musical notes, the same as a melody.

clue.text: Volume offering, by the way, charity

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Volume offering, by the way, charity (4,2,6)'. PS (by the way) + ALMS (charity) give PSALMS, but no word gives BOOK OF cleanly: 'Volume' would have to give BOOK and 'offering' OF, and 'offering' does not mean 'of'; likely an OCR garble.
annotationWithheld.clue: Volume offering, by the way, charity

clue.text: Student for example, a student who's within the law

parts.note: L, the learner plate shown by a learner driver, stands for a student
L again, the learner's letter

explanation.surface: A law student, for instance, who keeps on the right side of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Student' appears twice, each giving L for a learner.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lawful or permitted by statute is described as legal.

clue.text: Broad examination exists of his sort of thought

definitions.text: Broad examination exists of his sort of thought

parts.words: Broad examination exists of his sort of thought
parts.note: C. D. Broad, the Cambridge philosopher, wrote a study called Scientific Thought, an examination of the kind of thinking done by a researcher in the sciences

explanation.surface: A wide-ranging study of one person's way of thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broad' looks like an adjective meaning wide, but it is the philosopher C. D. Broad, whose book Scientific Thought (1923) examines this person's way of thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad's book studies scientific thought, the way of reasoning used by someone who does experimental research.

clue.text: Composer seen in the Waldorf, finally

indicators.note: the composer's name can be seen inside the run of letters across the end of Waldorf and the start of finally

explanation.surface: A composer spotted at last in the Waldorf hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' marks the hidden word, which spans the join of 'Waldorf' and 'finally'. 'finally' looks like an indicator for a last letter but only supplies letters. Carl Orff wrote Carmina Burana.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Orff was the German composer best known for the cantata Carmina Burana.

clue.text: Novel of some critical significance

explanation.surface: A book that matters a great deal to critics.
explanation.walkthrough: The Razor's Edge (1944) is Somerset Maugham's novel; to be on a razor's edge is to be at a critical, precarious point.
explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's novel bears this title, and the phrase also means a knife-edge situation where everything hangs in the balance.

clue.text: But Conrad, Joyce, Thomas and Evelyn treated them as family

definitions.text: But Conrad, Joyce, Thomas and Evelyn treated them as family

parts.words: But Conrad, Joyce, Thomas and Evelyn treated them as family
parts.note: Joseph Conrad, James Joyce, Dylan Thomas and John Evelyn all have surnames that are usually given names, so they used given names as family names

explanation.surface: Four writers who treated something as one of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad, Joyce, Thomas and Evelyn are all surnames of writers that are more often used as given names.
explanation.definitionFit: Each writer's surname is the kind of name normally given at christening, so these writers used christian names as family names.

clue.text: Sort of language heard in Budapest as well as Siberia

definitions.text: Sort of language heard in Budapest as well as Siberia

parts.words: Sort of language heard in Budapest as well as Siberia
parts.note: Hungarian, spoken in Budapest, belongs to the same language family as several tongues of western Siberia and Finland

explanation.surface: A kind of language spoken both in Hungary and in Siberia.
explanation.definitionFit: Hungarian and its distant Siberian relatives Khanty and Mansi make up the Ugric branch of the Uralic family, alongside Finnish.

clue.text: Emperor makes use of these letters first and last they are in credit

indicators.note: are in places the alphabet's end letters inside the credit abbreviation

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
Z is the last letter of the alphabet
A is the first letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: An emperor who makes good use of his letters of credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'these letters first and last' points to the alphabet: Z (the last) then A (the first), which 'are in' CR, the abbreviation for credit.
explanation.definitionFit: The title tsar, sometimes spelt with a C and Z, was used by the Russian emperors.

clue.text: Eliot's had shape without form, shade without colour

definitions.text: Eliot's had shape without form, shade without colour

parts.words: Eliot's had shape without form, shade without colour
parts.note: the quoted words come from T. S. Eliot's 1925 poem describing figures who are stuffed and empty inside

explanation.surface: A description of figures in Eliot who have outline but no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shape without form, shade without colour' is a line from T. S. Eliot's 1925 poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poem describes its empty, stuffed figures as having shape without form and shade without colour.

clue.text: Novelist may be strolling, huh? (Perhaps to his 20)

indicators.note: may be says the letters could become something else, so they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A novelist out for a stroll, letting out a puzzled 'huh?'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals an anagram of STROLLINGHUH. The bracket points to 20, The Swimming-Pool Library, Alan Hollinghurst's first novel (1988).
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Hollinghurst is the English writer of The Line of Beauty and The Swimming-Pool Library.

clue.text: Dons no longer young but still offering fine art

explanation.surface: Elderly university teachers who still deal in fine art.
explanation.walkthrough: Dons are university teachers, masters of colleges; once old, they are old masters. The same phrase names great European painters of before about 1800 and their works.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged college dons are literally elderly masters, and the phrase also names great European painters before about 1800 and their pictures.

clue.text: Morton's doctor with squint

explanation.surface: A doctor in Morton's writing who has a squint.
explanation.walkthrough: J. B. Morton wrote the Beachcomber humour column in the Daily Express, featuring the inventor Dr Strabismus (Whom God Preserve) of Utrecht.
explanation.definitionFit: Morton's absurd inventor bears this name, and it is also the medical term for an eye misalignment, a squint.

clue.text: Odyssey's acquiescent exiles hop gaol, it is absurd

indicators.note: is absurd tells us the phrase makes no sense as it stands, so its letters must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Exiles from the Odyssey escaping from prison, which seems ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is absurd' signals an anagram of HOPGAOLIT. In the Odyssey the lotus-eaters lose all wish to go home.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's lotus-eaters, the Lotophagi, live in drugged content and never leave their land, as passive and acquiescent as exiles.

clue.text: Parts of characters on the up

definitions.text: Parts of characters on the up

parts.words: Parts of characters on the up
parts.note: letters such as b, d and h have strokes rising above the body of the lower-case letter; the phrase also reads as people climbing

explanation.surface: Bits of people who are rising in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' looks like people, but here it means printed letters; the rising strokes of b, d, h and k are named for going up.
explanation.definitionFit: In typography the upward strokes of letters like b and d are named for climbing, so they are parts of letters that go up.

clue.text: I will neither yield to the songs of the siren nor the voice of the (George Chapman, Eastward Ho)

definitions.text: I will neither yield to the songs of the siren nor the voice of the (George Chapman, Eastward Ho)

parts.words: I will neither yield to the songs of the siren nor the voice of the (George Chapman, Eastward Ho)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the laughing animal believed to lure people with a human voice

explanation.surface: A line from the play Eastward Ho with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastward Ho (1605) was written by Chapman, Jonson and Marston. Old natural history held that this beast imitated human voices to lure victims.
explanation.definitionFit: Old bestiaries claimed this scavenging African beast could mimic a human voice to entice its prey, making it a companion to the siren.

clue.text: Exceptional horse from Middle-earth, possibly a mare

indicators.note: possibly says the words could be some other arrangement, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A remarkable horse from Tolkien's world that might be a female.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals an anagram of AMARE. In Tolkien the mearas are the great horses of Rohan, such as Shadowfax.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tolkien's Lord of the Rings the mearas are the noblest horses of Rohan, Shadowfax chief among them.

clue.text: Ashmole's had a number of peers

definitions.text: Ashmole's had a number of peers

parts.words: Ashmole's had a number of peers
parts.note: Elias Ashmole, the antiquary and herald, compiled a list of the noble Knights of the Garter in his history of the Order

explanation.surface: Elias Ashmole's possessed many lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Elias Ashmole, founder of Oxford's Ashmolean Museum, wrote a history of the Order of the Garter listing its noble knights.
explanation.definitionFit: A systematic list of items or persons, such as Ashmole's roll of Garter knights, is a register containing many names.

clue.text: Library work of 12, pleasant to dip into

definitions.text: Library work of 12, pleasant to dip into

parts.words: Library work of 12, pleasant to dip into
parts.note: with Library it gives the title of a novel by the writer at 12, and the place itself is pleasant to plunge into

explanation.surface: A book from a library that is nice to browse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dip into' suggests browsing a book, but the answer is a place for a dip; with 'Library' it names Hollinghurst's 1988 novel The Swimming-Pool Library.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollinghurst's novel takes its title from a London club's bathing pool, and such a pool is literally pleasant to dip into.

clue.text: Nobel prizewinning suggested exclusion (on principle) ()

parts.note: the Nobel physicist Wolfgang who proposed that no two electrons can share the same quantum state, the exclusion principle

explanation.surface: A Nobel winner who proposed shutting something out as a matter of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolfgang Pauli won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics for the exclusion principle; 'on principle' looks like a moral stance but names the law.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli formulated the exclusion principle and won the 1945 Nobel Prize for it.

clue.text: Poet loses opening bet

indicators.note: loses opening says the poet's name gives up its first letter

parts.note: Dante Alighieri is the Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A poet who loses his first wager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses opening' removes the D from DANTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stake put into the pot before the cards are dealt in poker is a bet made in advance.

clue.text: "As it —, it ain't. That's logic." (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "As it —, it ain't. That's logic." (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "As it —, it ain't. That's logic." (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: Tweedledee's line in Through the Looking-Glass, needing a short negative verb to fill the blank

explanation.surface: Tweedledee's nonsense logic from Lewis Carroll with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledee says in Through the Looking-Glass: 'if it was so, it might be; and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't, it ain't. That's logic.'
explanation.definitionFit: The blank needs the contracted negative of the verb to be, matching the colloquial 'ain't' that follows.

clue.text: The Spanish-manuscript dealt with diseased trees

parts.note: el is the Spanish masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A Spanish manuscript about sick trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dealt with' is a link. Britain's elms were destroyed by Dutch elm disease from the 1960s, so 'diseased trees' describes them fairly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch elm disease killed most of Britain's mature elms, the trees best known for that blight.

clue.text: american poet in an enormous room, used the lower sort, just in case

definitions.text: american poet in an enormous room, used the lower sort, just in case

parts.words: american poet in an enormous room, used the lower sort, just in case
parts.note: the US poet wrote the prison memoir The Enormous Room and signed his name without capitals, in lower case

explanation.surface: An American poet in a huge room who chose the humbler kind, just to be safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just in case' sounds like caution but means letter case: the poet often wrote his name in lower case, and the clue itself starts with a small 'american'. The Enormous Room (1922) is his memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Estlin Cummings, the American modernist poet, wrote The Enormous Room and was famous for lower-case typography.

clue.text: Consensus slowly reveals Feuchtwanger's character

indicators.note: reveals says the name is shown inside the run across the end of Consensus and the start of slowly

explanation.surface: A consensus slowly uncovers a character in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reveals' marks the hidden name across 'Consensus slowly'. Lion Feuchtwanger's novel Jud Süß (1925) is about the court financier Joseph Süß Oppenheimer.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Süß Oppenheimer is the title figure of Lion Feuchtwanger's historical novel Jud Süß.

clue.text: Lyons's was in Utopia

parts.note: Eugene Lyons, an American journalist, titled his 1937 book on six years as a correspondent in Soviet Russia with this word followed by in Utopia

explanation.surface: Lyons's something took place in an ideal land.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Lyons's book Assignment in Utopia (1937) describes his disillusioning posting to Soviet Moscow.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist's posting is a task given to them, and Lyons titled his Moscow memoir after it.
